learningObjectives.title: Characters (the Birlings, Gerald, the Inspector, Eva Smith)

questions.q: In which year is 'An Inspector Calls' set?
questions.explain: The play is set in 1912, two years before the First World War, during the complacent Edwardian era.

questions.q: In which year did J.B. Priestley write the play?
questions.explain: Priestley wrote the play in 1945, at the end of the Second World War, when Britain was rebuilding and debating social responsibility.

questions.q: What is the name of the young working-class woman whose death the Inspector investigates?
options: Eva Smith
Sybil Birling
Sheila Croft
Edna Renton
questions.explain: Eva Smith is the working-class woman whose suicide connects all the Birlings and Gerald.

questions.q: What name did Eva Smith use during her relationship with Gerald Croft?
options: Daisy Renton
Edna Birling
Alice Grey
Sarah Peck
questions.explain: Eva Smith used the name Daisy Renton when Gerald met her at the Palace bar and made her his mistress.

questions.q: How does Eva Smith die?
options: She drinks strong disinfectant
She drowns in a river
She is killed in a factory accident
She dies of an illness
questions.explain: Eva Smith commits suicide by swallowing strong disinfectant, which burns her insides out.

questions.q: What is the surname of the Inspector who calls on the Birlings?
options: Goole
Croft
Renton
Birling
questions.explain: The Inspector is named Goole, a homophone of 'ghoul' that hints at his mysterious, possibly supernatural nature.

questions.q: To whom is Sheila Birling engaged at the start of the play?
options: Gerald Croft
Eric Birling
Inspector Goole
Arthur Birling
questions.explain: Sheila is engaged to Gerald Croft, whose family owns a rival firm, Crofts Limited.

questions.q: Which ship does Arthur Birling confidently describe as 'unsinkable'?
options: The Titanic
The Lusitania
The Mauretania
The Britannic
questions.explain: Birling calls the Titanic 'absolutely unsinkable', an example of dramatic irony as the audience knows it sank in 1912.

questions.q: What role does Mrs Sybil Birling hold that connects her to Eva Smith?
options: Chair of a women's charity organisation
Owner of Milwards store
Manager of the Palace bar
A magistrate
questions.explain: Mrs Birling chairs the Brumley Women's Charity Organisation and refused Eva Smith the help she requested.

questions.q: Why did Sheila Birling have Eva Smith dismissed from Milwards?
options: Out of jealousy over a dress
For stealing money
For being rude to a customer
For arriving late to work
questions.explain: Sheila had Eva sacked in a jealous temper because a dress suited Eva better than it suited her.

questions.q: What is the main effect of the play's cyclical structure, ending with news of another inspector calling?
options: It suggests the family will be forced to face their guilt again
It proves the first Inspector was a real policeman
It shows the family has fully reformed
It confirms Eva Smith is still alive
questions.explain: The final phone call restarts the cycle, implying the unrepentant Birlings will have to confront their responsibility once more.

questions.q: Why does Priestley give Birling confident speeches denying the possibility of war?
options: To use dramatic irony that undermines Birling's judgement
To show Birling is a reliable narrator
To praise Birling's political wisdom
To provide accurate historical prediction
questions.explain: The 1945 audience knew two world wars followed, so Birling's confident predictions expose him as foolish and untrustworthy.

questions.q: How does Sheila change over the course of the play?
options: She accepts responsibility and becomes more socially aware
She becomes more like her complacent parents
She refuses to believe any wrongdoing occurred
She loses all sense of guilt by the end
questions.explain: Sheila matures, feels genuine guilt, and embraces the Inspector's message of collective responsibility.

questions.q: What does the Inspector mean by 'We are members of one body. We are responsible for each other'?
options: Society is interconnected and people must care for one another
The Birlings are literally related to Eva Smith
Only families have duties to each other
Business owners should ignore their workers
questions.explain: The Inspector voices Priestley's socialist theme that individuals share collective responsibility for society's welfare.

questions.q: What does the Inspector's warning of 'fire and blood and anguish' most likely foreshadow?
options: The suffering of the two world wars
A fire at the Birling factory
Eva Smith's method of suicide
The sinking of the Titanic
questions.explain: The phrase foreshadows the violence of the world wars that follow if society refuses to learn responsibility.

questions.q: How does Priestley present the divide between the older and younger Birlings?
options: The younger generation accept responsibility while the older resist change
Both generations reject the Inspector's message equally
The older generation are the most remorseful
Only Gerald learns from the events
questions.explain: Sheila and Eric are changed by the Inspector, whereas Arthur and Sybil cling to their old attitudes, showing hope in the young.

questions.q: What does Arthur Birling's belief that 'a man has to make his own way' reveal about his values?
options: His capitalist, individualist outlook
His commitment to socialism
His belief in collective responsibility
His concern for his workers' welfare
questions.explain: Birling's phrase encapsulates his self-interested, capitalist ideology, which the play sets up to be criticised.

questions.q: Why did Priestley set the play in 1912 but write it for a 1945 audience?
options: To contrast Edwardian complacency with post-war hopes for social change
Because he wanted an accurate historical documentary
To avoid any political message
Because 1912 was the year the play was first performed
questions.explain: The 1912 setting exposes pre-war class complacency, while the 1945 audience was ready to build a fairer, more responsible society.

questions.q: Eric admits he took money from his father's office. What does this action most reveal about his character?
options: He feels a flawed sense of responsibility towards Eva but acts wrongly
He is entirely indifferent to Eva's plight
He is a careful and law-abiding young man
He shares his father's cold business values
questions.explain: Eric's theft to support Eva shows a misguided attempt to help, marking him as guilty yet capable of remorse.

questions.q: A student argues that Eva Smith symbolises the vulnerability of working-class women. Which evidence best supports this?
options: She is exploited in turn by employers and by wealthy men
She refuses all help offered to her
She is a member of the Birling family
She holds a powerful position in Brumley
questions.explain: Eva's exploitation by Birling, Sheila, Gerald, Eric and Mrs Birling shows how class and gender left working-class women powerless.

questions.q: How would a 1945 audience, voting in a new welfare state, most likely respond to the Inspector's message?
options: Sympathetically, as it echoed calls for collective social care
With hostility, as they rejected any social reform
With indifference, as the ideas were irrelevant to them
By agreeing with Birling's individualism
questions.explain: The 1945 audience, embracing the emerging welfare state, would recognise the Inspector's plea for shared responsibility.

specSource: AQA GCSE English Literature (8702) specification; An Inspector Calls
